passage:
Sunaina: The insurance renewal notice came. Due next month.
Hrithik: Again?? That wrecked our March last time.
Sunaina: And Diwali. And the geyser repair in June. Every year the same three things blow up the budget.
Hrithik: They're not really surprises though. We just forget they're yearly.
Sunaina: What if we put a little aside every month for exactly those? Insurance, festivals, repairs. Its own pot.
Hrithik: So when the bill comes the money's already there.
Sunaina: Not an emergency. Just a Tuesday.
Hrithik: Love it. Start this month? 🙂
Sunaina: Starting today 🙂

qa.q: Which three yearly costs did Sunaina name?
qa.a: The insurance renewal, Diwali and the geyser repair in June.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's "Again??" suggest about how Hrithik feels?
qa.a: It suggests Hrithik feels frustrated and a little dreading the bill, remembering how it wrecked March.

qa.q: What other approach could help them set the right amount for the pot?
qa.a: They could look at last year's statements to see what each yearly cost really was and spread that over the twelve months.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt about the yearly bills before the idea?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt stressed by the same three costs upsetting the budget every year, which is why the idea came quickly.

grounding: Sunaina and Hrithik notice yearly costs like insurance, festivals and repairs upset monthly plans, so they put a little aside each month.

passage:
In their small house above the Lunglei market, Lalremsiami kept the monthly accounts in a school notebook. Every month looked fine on paper. Then October came: the scooter insurance. December: Christmas, new clothes for the children, the church offering. March: the roof leaked again. Each time the plan fell apart, and Pankaj borrowed from his brother.
One evening she turned back through two years of pages and said, half to herself, "These aren't surprises. They come every year. We just pretend they don't." She added them up and divided by twelve.
"So we put a little aside every month, in a separate tin, only for these," she told Pankaj. "Then when the insurance letter comes, it's just a bill."
Pankaj looked doubtful. "Every month? Even when nothing's due?"
"Especially then."

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami say about the yearly costs?
qa.a: "These aren't surprises. They come every year. We just pretend they don't."

qa.q: What does Pankaj's doubtful look suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He is unsure and a bit reluctant to set money aside in months when nothing is due.

qa.q: What else could help the tin plan work?
qa.a: They could list the yearly costs and their months at the front of the notebook and check the tin together whenever one of them comes due.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's brother be affected by the new tin?
qa.a: His brother may no longer be asked for a loan every time a yearly bill arrives, which could ease things between the brothers.

grounding: It shows a couple realising that yearly costs like insurance, festivals and repairs keep breaking their monthly plan and deciding to set a little aside each month for them.

passage:
Diego and Ada had a spreadsheet for their flat in Valencia that balanced beautifully, eleven months a year. Then came the car insurance in February, the Christmas gifts, and the boiler repair that happened every autumn without fail. Each time, they dipped into savings and felt as if they had failed.
One Sunday Ada spread the year's bank statements across the floor and circled every "surprise" in red. "Diego, look. The boiler man came in October last year too. The insurance is always February. We're acting shocked by the calendar."
They added up the red circles, divided by twelve and opened a small separate account called Predictable Surprises. A little went into it every month.
When the insurance renewal arrived the next February, Diego paid it, shrugged and went back to his coffee.

qa.q: What did they call the separate account?
How did Ada feel when she said they were acting shocked by the calendar?
qa.a: Ada felt a mix of frustration and relief: frustrated at the pattern, relieved that it was predictable and could be planned for.

qa.q: What else could Ada and Diego do to keep the account working?
qa.a: They could look over the red-circle list each year, add any new regular costs, and change the monthly amount together.

qa.q: How is the February insurance different for Diego afterwards?
qa.a: It becomes just a bill he pays with a shrug instead of another small crisis.

grounding: It shows a couple noticing that annual costs like insurance, gifts and repairs upset their monthly plan and setting aside a small monthly amount so the bills stop feeling like emergencies.
